charts.title: How the test was built: five models, one planted check and two null controls.
charts.takeaway: The combined formula had to beat flexible prospect theory by 0.005 in cross-validated R² in both settings. It did so in neither.
charts.n: 1,928 choice problems without feedback and 9,831 with feedback (choices13k, aggregate choice rates)

steps.detail: Data simulated from a known model. Model selection had to pick that model in more than 80 percent of sets.

steps.detail: Gain −0.011 without feedback and 0.0009 with it.

charts.title: Held-out fit of each model, without and with feedback.
charts.takeaway: Combined formula 0.634 against flexible prospect theory 0.645 without feedback, and 0.597 against 0.596 with it. The bar was a gain of 0.005.
charts.units: cross-validated R²: share of variance in choice rates explained on problems held out of the fit; higher is better
charts.n: 1,928 choice problems without feedback and 9,831 with feedback (choices13k, aggregate choice rates)
charts.no_interval: The result file holds one cross-validated R² per model and setting, with no interval.
charts.baseline: Flexible prospect theory, and the noise ceiling (the best R² the sampling noise in the rates allows)
charts.threshold: Combined formula ahead of flexible prospect theory by at least 0.005 in cross-validated R²
charts.planted: Held: model selection picked the planted model in 6 of 6 simulated data sets
charts.ruled_out: A gain of 0.005 or more over flexible prospect theory: the measured gains are −0.011 without feedback and 0.0009 with feedback

charts.title: Without feedback: the joint gain of the four added terms against two null controls.
charts.takeaway: The gain is 7.6 in deviance, below the 95th percentile of both controls (52.0 and 58.9).
charts.units: deviance gain: drop in misfit when the four terms are added to prospect theory; higher means the terms explain more
charts.n: 1,928 problems without feedback; 200 and 100 control draws
charts.interval: 5th to 95th percentile of the control draws
charts.baseline: Two null controls in which the added terms carry no information
charts.threshold: Joint gain above the 95th percentile of each control
charts.ruled_out: A joint gain beyond what the nulls produce: 7.6 sits below 52.0 (p 0.82) and 58.9 (p 0.89)

axis.label: joint deviance gain (higher means the terms explain more)

rows.label: Added terms permuted across problems
rows.note: real 7.6; control 3.9 to 52.0, mean 20.9; p 0.82 from 200 draws

rows.note: real 7.6; control 3.8 to 58.9, mean 24.0; p 0.89 from 100 draws

charts.title: Fitted loss aversion in each setting.
charts.takeaway: Loss aversion is 1.16 without feedback and 0.89 with it: far below the classic 2.25, and below 1 once people see outcomes.
charts.units: loss aversion λ: how much more a loss weighs than an equal gain; 1 means equal weight
charts.n: 1,928 choice problems without feedback and 9,831 with feedback (choices13k, aggregate choice rates)
charts.baseline: λ = 1 (losses and gains weigh the same) and λ = 2.25 (Tversky and Kahneman's estimate)
charts.threshold: Without feedback: interval above 1 and below 2.25. Both held.
series_names: Loss aversion fitted in cumulative prospect theory

axis.label: loss aversion λ (1 means losses and gains weigh the same)
